title: Jacobian Scopes: A Unified Geometric Framework for Token-Level LLM Attribution
claim: A single perturb-linearize-project procedure over a model's output space yields a family of attribution variants, each probing a different output feature.
layout: 3 stacked rows (a,b,c), each left-to-right, separated by horizontal rules
description: A rounded-border figure with three stacked panels separated by horizontal lines. Panel a shows the tokens "words are represented as" (x1 to x4) with arrows pointing into them. These feed a blue LLM box, then a blue hidden-state vector y, then a blue bar-chart histogram labeled "vectors", with p = softmax(Wy) beneath. Panel b shows three steps labeled perturb, linearize and project. Perturb is a small noise ball around x_t. Linearize is a boxed equation, J_t = ∂y/∂x_t and δy ≈ J_t δx_t. Project is a blue ellipse of δy with arrows for ŷ (temperature direction), w_target, and u1 (principal Fisher direction). Panel c shows three histograms titled Semantic, Fisher and Temperature Scope. A red bar highlights the target logit, a red-and-blue stacked bar shows the most KL-sensitive direction, and a red curve with outward arrows shows peak width. The eye goes first to the red highlights in panel c.
caption: Overview of Jacobian Scopes. (a) An autoregressive LLM maps an input token sequence to a hidden state $\bm{y}$, which is decoded into a predictive distribution over the vocabulary. (b) A small perturbation to any input token is propagated to the output via the Jacobian $\bm{J}_t$, then projected onto a direction $\bm{v}$ in output space; the magnitude of this projection defines the token's influence score, computable in a single backward pass. The three Scopes correspond to $\bm{v} = \bm{w}_\mathrm{target}$ (target unembedding row), $\bm{v} = \bm{u}_1$ (principal Fisher direction), and $\bm{v} = \hat{\bm{y}}$ (normalized hidden state). (c) The three Jacobian Scope variants each target a different feature of the model's output: Semantic Scope asks which input tokens drive the predicted probability of a specific target word; Fisher Scope asks which tokens most change the overall shape of the predicted distribution; and Temperature Scope asks which tokens control the model's confidence, i.e., how sharply peaked the distribution is.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) make next-token predictions based on clues present in their context, such as semantic descriptions and in-context examples. Yet, elucidating which prior tokens most strongly influence a given prediction remains challenging due to the proliferation of layers and attention heads in modern architectures. We propose Jacobian Scopes, a suite of gradient-based, token level causal attribution methods for interpreting LLM predictions. Grounded in perturbation theory and information geometry, Jacobian Scopes quantify how input tokens influence various aspects of a model's prediction, such as specific logits, the full predictive distribution, and model uncertainty (effective temperature). Through case studies spanning instruction understanding, translation, and in-context learning (ICL), we demonstrate how Jacobian Scopes reveal implicit political biases, uncover word- and phrase-level translation strategies, and shed light on recently debated mechanisms underlying in-context time-series forecasting. On token-ablation faithfulness benchmarks (LAMBADA and IWSLT2017) across six LLMs, the distribution-level Fisher and Temperature Scopes significantly outperform established gradient-based attribution methods in 10 of 12 model-dataset settings. To facilitate exploration of Jacobian Scopes on custom text, we open-source our implementations and provide a cloud-hosted interactive demo at https://huggingface.co/spaces/Typony/JacobianScopes.
